# Sources and evidence, verified 2026-09-21

Evidence file for the seo-audit skill. Every check the script runs, and every sentence the report writes, should be traceable to a row here. If a row is not here, the claim is not ours to make.

## How to use this file

- Before adding a check, find the fact in section 1. If it is not there, it is not verified.
- Before writing finding text, read section 2. Those are the beliefs that make an auditor confidently wrong.
- Before assigning a severity, read the calibration paragraph below and section 3.
- Dates are the dates the source page showed on 2026-09-21. Where a source published no date, the cell says "no date". Nothing here was inferred, extrapolated or rounded.

## Evidence classes

- **(a)** documented by the platform or spec owner. The strongest class. A quoted sentence from Google, Microsoft, Cloudflare, an RFC, a W3C spec or a vendor's own crawler docs.
- **(b)** credible measurement or study. Real data, but with a sample, a method and a bias.
- **(c)** folklore, vendor marketing, or inference with no published data. Never the basis of a scored finding.
- **(a-archived)** platform-authored, snapshot-dated in the Wayback Machine, no longer published.
- **(a-pending)** platform-authored, in the platform's own docs repo, unmerged.
- **unverified** means the research looked and could not confirm from a primary source. Keep that label. Do not upgrade it because a secondary blog repeats it.

## The central calibration finding

An HTML-only audit scores the weaker half of the evidence, and the report should say so. In the one industry study doing real multivariate attribution (SE Ranking, 2,328,533 pages, XGBoost with SHAP, 2025-12-15), off-page factors move median AI citations 2.4 to 6.4 (domain traffic) and 2.5 to 6.8 (referring domains), while on-page factors move them 4.1 to 5.1 (content length) and 4.4 to 4.9 (an FAQ block). Ahrefs' 75,000-brand correlation puts branded web mentions at Spearman 0.664 and backlinks at 0.218. None of that is fixable from HTML. At the same time AI referral traffic is about 1% of site traffic (Conductor, 1,215 enterprise domains, 3.3B sessions, 2026-07-06: 1.08%; Ahrefs, 81,947 sites, 2025-06-26: 0.25%). So AI-search findings must not outrank crawlability or Core Web Vitals in the severity ordering, and "has schema", "has llms.txt" and similar must never be scored as AI visibility.

## 1.2 robots.txt semantics and status handling

| Fact | Auditor use | Source | Date | Class |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Supported fields are exactly four: `user-agent`, `allow`, `disallow`, `sitemap`. "Other fields such as `crawl-delay` aren't supported" at Google | Parse only four; report `crawl-delay` as info, not error | robots-txt-spec | 2026-08-31 | (a) |
| "User agent specific groups and global groups (`*`) are not combined." A `Googlebot` group means `*` never applies to Googlebot | The single most common robots-parser bug | same | 2026-08-31 | (a) |
| Most specific rule wins by path length; on conflict Google uses the least restrictive rule. Field names and user-agent values case-insensitive, **path values case-sensitive**, paths must start with `/`. `*` = zero or more chars, `$` = end, trailing `*` ignored | Matcher implementation | same | 2026-08-31 | (a) |
| Size limit exactly 500 KiB; content past it ignored. UTF-8; BOM ignored; must be at host root, never a subdirectory; scoped to host + protocol + port | Size and location checks | same, plus RFC 9309 | 2026-08-31 | (a) |
| 5xx: "the crawler MUST assume complete disallow" (RFC 9309). Google stops crawling 12 h, uses the cached copy up to 30 days, then treats the site as unrestricted if otherwise available | robots.txt 5xx is a **critical** finding | RFC 9309 + robots-txt-spec | 2022-09 / 2026-08-31 | (a) |
| 4xx except 429 treated as "no robots.txt exists", so no restrictions. "Don't use 401 and 403 status codes for limiting the crawl rate." 429 is a server error. DNS, timeout, reset and chunking errors are server errors | Status-specific severities | same | 2026-08-31 | (a) |
| robots.txt follows at least five redirect hops, then treats it as 404. Logical redirects (frames, JS, meta refresh) not followed | Hop count check | same | 2026-08-31 | (a) |
| robots.txt cached up to 24 h; `Cache-Control: max-age` can lengthen or shorten | Explains slow propagation | same | 2026-08-31 | (a) |
| A `sitemap:` line between two `user-agent:` lines does not split the group | Parser detail | same | 2026-08-31 | (a) |
| A robots.txt served as `text/html` (an SPA catch-all) is the most common real-world robots.txt bug | High severity; test `Content-Type` and whether the body starts with `<` | derived from the spec plus observed practice | 2026-09-21 | (a)/(b) |
| Disallowed URLs can still be indexed URL-only: "Google can't index the content of pages which are disallowed for crawling, but it may still index the URL" | Explains "indexed though blocked" | same | 2026-08-31 | (a) |

## 1.3 AI-preference signals: Content-Signal and Content-Usage

These are two different mechanisms with confusingly similar names. A site can carry both, and contradictions between them are worth a medium finding.

| Mechanism | Exact syntax | Vocabulary | Values | Status | Source | Date | Class |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Content Signals Policy** (Cloudflare) | A `Content-Signal:` line inside a robots.txt group, comma-delimited: `Content-Signal: search=yes, ai-train=no` | `search`, `ai-input`, `ai-train` (Cloudflare's managed block also emits an experimental `use=reference`) | `yes` / `no`; **absent "neither grants nor restricts permission"** | Published policy, not a standards-track document | https://blog.cloudflare.com/content-signals-policy/ ; https://contentsignals.org/ | 2025-09-24 | (a) |
| `search` definition | "building a search index and providing search results… **Search does not include providing AI-generated search summaries**" | n/a | n/a | n/a | contentsignals.org | 2025-09-24 | (a) |
| `ai-input` definition | "inputting content into one or more AI models (e.g., retrieval augmented generation, grounding, or other real-time taking of content for generative AI search answers)" | n/a | n/a | n/a | contentsignals.org | 2025-09-24 | (a) |
| `ai-train` definition | "training or fine-tuning AI models" | n/a | n/a | n/a | contentsignals.org | 2025-09-24 | (a) |
| **IETF `Content-Usage`** | HTTP response header as a Structured Fields Dictionary: `Content-Usage: train-ai=n`. Also a robots.txt directive with an **optional path pattern before the preference**: `Content-Usage: /ai-ok/ train-ai=y` | `train-ai`, `ai-use`, `search` | `y` / `n`; absent = preference unknown | `draft-ietf-aipref-vocab-08` (2026-09-14) and `draft-ietf-aipref-attach-05` (2026-08-19, expires 2027-02-20). Active WG drafts, intended Proposed Standard. **Neither is an RFC. Do not call it a standard** | https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-aipref-vocab/ ; https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-aipref-attach/ | 2026-09-14 / 2026-08-19 | (a) |
| `train-ai` | "Using an asset to modify the learned parameters of a generative AI model." Excludes non-generative tasks | n/a | n/a | n/a | vocab-08 | 2026-09-14 | (a) |
| `ai-use` | "Using an asset as input to a generative AI model, where the asset is not directly provided by the user." Not training | n/a | n/a | n/a | vocab-08 | 2026-09-14 | (a) |
| `search` (IETF) | "Using an asset in an application where the primary purpose… is to select assets and direct users to the location of those assets." Requires links back and relevance-only excerpts | n/a | n/a | n/a | vocab-08 | 2026-09-14 | (a) |
| Attachment mechanisms are **only two**: the HTTP header and the robots.txt directive. There is no HTML meta or link form in the draft | Do not probe for a meta tag | n/a | n/a | n/a | attach-05 | 2026-08-19 | (a) |
| Naming collision | `Content-Signal` (Cloudflare, robots.txt only, `yes`/`no`, `search`/`ai-input`/`ai-train`) is not `Content-Usage` (IETF, robots.txt + header, `y`/`n`, `search`/`ai-use`/`train-ai`) | Parse both; flag e.g. `ai-train=no` next to `train-ai=y` as a medium contradiction | n/a | n/a | n/a | n/a | (a) |
| `Content-Signal` as an HTTP header | Exists only on Cloudflare Markdown for Agents responses, not as a general surface | n/a | n/a | Real but narrow, not general. Confidence medium | https://developers.cloudflare.com/fundamentals/reference/markdown-for-agents/ | 2026-02-12 | (a), medium |

- **No Copilot crawler exists.** Microsoft's crawlers page lists five crawlers, none Copilot-specific, so never check for a "Copilot-bot" robots.txt token. Source: https://www.bing.com/webmasters/help/which-crawlers-does-bing-use-8c184ec0 (no date). Class (a), verified negative.
- **Brave.** Brave Search's crawler "deliberately does not advertise a differentiated UA" because, in Brave's words, "we must avoid discrimination from websites that allow only Google to crawl them". Brave also states that if a page is not crawlable by Googlebot, Brave's bot will not crawl it either. You therefore cannot detect or selectively allow Brave by User-Agent. Source: https://search.brave.com/help/brave-search-crawler (no date). Class (a).
- **Cohere.** No active crawler: "We do not use Cohere bots or user agents for the purpose of crawling or scraping web content to train generative AI foundation models at this time." The table shows N/A and a future bot would be `Coherebot`. Blocking `cohere-ai` or `cohere-training-data-crawler` is cargo cult. Source: https://docs.cohere.com/docs/cohere-web-crawlers (no date). Class (a).
- **xAI and Grok.** No crawler documentation found on x.ai or docs.x.ai on 2026-09-21. A Grok reply on X claiming Grok uses an iPhone UA to avoid blocks is not documentation. Report as "xAI publishes no crawler documentation we could find". Class (c).

## 1.5 Cloudflare edge behaviors and wire signatures

The robots.txt you fetch may not be the file the origin serves, and a 403 may be an edge decision.

| Signal | Meaning | Source | Date | Class |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `# BEGIN Cloudflare Managed content` … `# END Cloudflare Managed Content` (note the inconsistent capitalization; match case-insensitively) | Cloudflare **prepends** a managed block to the origin's robots.txt. Every `Disallow` above the end marker is Cloudflare's, not the owner's. The block carries `Content-signal: search=yes, ai-train=no, use=reference` and `Disallow: /` for Amazonbot, Applebot-Extended, Bytespider, CCBot, ClaudeBot, Google-Extended, GPTBot, meta-externalagent. Available on all plans | https://developers.cloudflare.com/bots/additional-configurations/managed-robots-txt/ | 2026-08-03 | (a) |
| `cf-ray` header, or `Server: cloudflare` | Zone is behind Cloudflare | universally observed | 2026-09-21 | (a)/(b) |
| `cf-mitigated: challenge` | The response is a Challenge page, not the site. "challenge" is the only valid value. Commonly accompanies 403 | https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-challenges/challenge-types/challenge-pages/detect-response/ | no date | (a) |
| HTTP 403 with a short plain-text body | AI Crawl Control's configured block. It can only enforce 403 or 402; changing the WAF rule code breaks enforcement | https://developers.cloudflare.com/ai-crawl-control/features/manage-ai-crawlers/ | no date | (a) |
| HTTP 402 + `crawler-price` response header | Pay per crawl. `crawler-charged` reports the amount billed; requests carry `crawler-exact-price` or `crawler-max-price` | https://developers.cloudflare.com/ai-crawl-control/features/pay-per-crawl/what-is-pay-per-crawl/ | no date | (a) |
| `Signature-Agent` request header + Web Bot Auth (Ed25519, IETF drafts `draft-meunier-web-bot-auth-architecture`, `-webbotauth-httpsig-protocol`, `-webbotauth-registry`) | Cryptographic bot verification | https://developers.cloudflare.com/bots/reference/bot-verification/web-bot-auth/ | no date | (a) |
| AI traffic is managed in three categories, Search / Agent / Training, each allow / block / "block only on pages that display ads" | An AI block can vary page by page | https://developers.cloudflare.com/changelog/post/2026-07-01-ai-traffic-options/ | 2026-07-01 | (a) |
| **2026-09-15 new defaults for new domains**: Training and Agent blocked on ad-displaying pages, Search allowed; multi-purpose Search+Training crawlers blocked for the Training activity | Six days before this file's verification date. Re-check before relying on it | same changelog | 2026-09-15 | (a) |

## 1.6 Structured data: what was retired, what survived

The June 2025 removal, verbatim from "Simplifying the search results page" (https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2025/06/simplifying-search-results, **June 12, 2025**, Henry Hsu): seven types, **Book Actions, Course Info, Claim Review, Estimated Salary, Learning Video, Special Announcement, Vehicle Listing**. Also verbatim: "This update won't affect how pages are ranked." An update appended **September 8, 2025** removed Search Console support for six of the seven (Book Actions excluded) from September 9, with API support through December 2025.

**Two of the seven survived.** Book Actions: changelog **2025-11-05**, "Removed the deprecation banner from Book actions documentation, as there's still a feature using the markup in Google Search." ClaimReview: the doc still returns 200 with a banner saying the markup "remains supported by the Factcheck Explorer Tool."

| Type | State | Date | Source | Class |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| FAQ rich result | Gone from Search **2026-05-07**; documentation removed 2026-06-15. There is no blog post, the changelog is the only announcement. 2023-08-08 had already limited it to "well-known, authoritative government and health websites" | 2026-05-07 | Search Central changelog 2026-05-08 and 2026-06-15; 301 to `/search/updates#removing-faq-rich-result` | (a) |
| HowTo rich result | Gone **2023-09-13**. But `HowToSection`, `HowToStep`, `HowToDirection`, `HowToTip` remain documented inside Recipe's `recipeInstructions`, and `HowTo` is still a valid `itemReviewed` type | 2023-09-13 | https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2023/08/howto-faq-changes (2023-08-08); 301 to `#how-to-deprecation` | (a) |
| Sitelinks searchbox | Gone 2024-11-21. `WebSite` + `potentialAction`/`SearchAction` is dead; `WebSite` + `name`/`alternateName` is alive and still drives site names. `nositelinkssearchbox` is archived as unused | 2024-10-21 | "Farewell, Sitelinks Search Box"; 301 to `#bye-sitelinkbox` | (a) |
| Practice problems | Removed in 2026 | 2026 | 301 to `#removing-practice-problems` | (a) |
| Course info, estimated salary, learning video, vehicle listing, special announcements | Removed | 2025-06-12 | 301s to `#simplification` | (a) |

| 2026 net change | **Minus two (FAQ, practice problems), plus zero.** Everything else in 2026 was properties and clarifications | 2026 | derived | (a) |
| The gallery, 25 types | Article, Breadcrumb, Carousel, Course list, Dataset, Discussion forum, Education Q&A, Employer aggregate rating, Event, Image metadata, Job posting, Local business, Math solver, Movie, Organization, Product, Profile page, Q&A, Recipe, Review snippet, Software app, Speakable, Subscription and paywalled content, Vacation rental, Video | 2026-06-15 | https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/structured-data/search-gallery | (a) |

| `Article` / `BlogPosting` / `NewsArticle` | **"There are no required properties."** Recommended: `author`, `author.name`, `author.url`, `dateModified`, `datePublished`, `headline`, `image`. Images 16x9, 4x3 or 1x1, minimum 50,000 pixels | /structured-data/article | 2026-09-08 | (a) |

That is all.** Recommended includes `aggregateRating`, `geo` (at least 5 decimal places), `openingHoursSpecification`, `priceRange`, `telephone`, `url`. 24 h = `00:00`/`23:59`; closed = both `00:00` | /structured-data/local-business | 2026-09-08 | (a) |
| `priceRange` | **Not deprecated.** Recommended, capped: "must be shorter than 100 characters" or Google will not show it | same | 2026-09-08 | (a) |

| `DiscussionForumPosting` | Required: `author`, `author.name`, `datePublished`, and one of `text`/`image`/`video` (not required when representing a post on another page with an external `url`) | /structured-data/discussion-forum | 2026-09-08 | (a) |

"If this property is not specified, Google will assume the content is human-generated." The first machine-readable AI-content disclosure property Google supports | changelog | 2026-03-24 | (a) |

### The self-serving review rule (the one that matters most for directory and awards sites)

Verbatim from `/structured-data/review-snippet` (**Last updated 2026-09-08**):

> "If the entity that's being reviewed controls the reviews about itself, their pages that use
> `LocalBusiness` or any other type of `Organization` structured data are ineligible for star
> review feature. For example, a review about entity A is placed on the website of entity A,
> either directly in their structured data or through an embedded third-party widget (for example,
> Google Business reviews or Facebook reviews widget)."
> "Ratings must be sourced directly from users."
> "Don't rely on human editors to create, curate, or compile ratings information for local
> businesses."

New July 2026 guideline (changelog **2026-07-24**), verbatim: "Don't include fake or undisclosed incentivized reviews on your page or in your structured data markup," naming reviews not based on genuine experience and reviews written in exchange for a benefit without clear disclosure.

| Property fact | Detail | Class |
|---|---|---|
| `Review` required | `author`, `itemReviewed`, `itemReviewed.name`, `reviewRating`, `reviewRating.ratingValue` | (a) |
| `AggregateRating` required | `itemReviewed`, `itemReviewed.name`, `ratingCount`, `reviewCount`, `ratingValue` | (a) |
| Author name | "must be a valid name… '50% off until Saturday' is not a valid name… shorter than 100 characters" | (a) |
| Defaults | bestRating defaults to 5, worstRating to 1; decimals "use a dot instead of a comma" | (a) |
| Prohibitions | "Don't aggregate reviews or ratings from other websites"; review content must be readable on the marked-up page; avoid multiple ways of indicating what is reviewed (changelog 2025-11-12) | (a) |
| LocalBusiness and Organization review support | Only for sites capturing reviews about **other** local businesses or organizations. For employers use `EmployerAggregateRating` | (a) |

## 1.7 Snippet controls, AI Overviews and AI Mode

`/crawling-indexing/robots-meta-tag`, **Last updated 2026-03-24**, is the authority.

| Fact | Auditor use | Class |
|---|---|---|
| "Google Search doesn't enforce placement of meta robots in the HTML head and will respect robots meta tags in the body section" | **Suppress** any "robots meta outside head" finding for Google | (a) |
| Only two crawler-specific meta `name` values are honored: `googlebot` and `googlebot-news`. All other names are ignored | Flag `name="bingbot"` style metas as inert at Google | (a) |
| `X-Robots-Tag` is repeatable or comma-separated with an optional UA prefix; header name, UA name and values are all case-insensitive | Header parsing | (a) |
| Conflict rule: "the more restrictive rule applies"; across differently-named tags, "the sum of the negative rules" | Collect every meta and header, then apply most-restrictive | (a) |
| Rules are only read if the URL is crawlable. A `Disallow`d page's `noindex` is never seen | High-severity combination finding | (a) |
| `nosnippet`: "applies to all forms of search results (at Google: web search, Google Images, Discover, AI Overviews, AI Mode) and will also prevent the content from being used as **a direct input for AI Overviews and AI Mode**" | Snippet controls are the AI levers | (a) |
| `max-snippet:[number]`: `0` is equivalent to `nosnippet`, `-1` lets Google choose, "ignored if no parseable [number] is specified", and it "will also limit how much of the content may be used as a direct input for AI Overviews and AI Mode" | Same | (a) |
| `max-image-preview` takes exactly three values: `none`, `standard`, `large`. **It does not name AI Overviews or AI Mode** | Any claim that it governs AI Overviews imagery is (c) | (a) |
| `max-video-preview:[number]`: `0` = static image only, `-1` = no limit | n/a | (a) |
| `indexifembedded` "only has an effect if it's accompanied by `noindex`" | Co-occurrence check | (a) |
| `unavailable_after:` accepts RFC 822, RFC 850 or ISO 8601; "Googlebot will decrease the crawl rate of the URL considerably after the specified date" | n/a | (a) |
| `noarchive`, `nocache`, `nositelinkssearchbox` are **dead at Google** | Info at Google, but see the Bing table: `noarchive` and `nocache` are live and AI-meaningful there | (a) |
| `data-nosnippet` is valid on **`span`, `div`, `section` only**; it is boolean ("any value specified is ignored", so `="false"` still suppresses); an unclosed element swallows everything after it; "do not add or remove the `data-nosnippet` attribute of existing nodes through JavaScript"; structured data inside it remains usable | Element-type and validity checks | (a) |
| "Read more" deep links (snippet doc, **2026-04-20**): content must be immediately visible, not behind an expander or tab; avoid JavaScript controlling scroll position on load; do not remove the hash fragment on load | n/a | (a) |

**What actually controls AI Overviews and AI Mode**, from `/search/docs/appearance/ai-features` (**Last updated 2025-12-10**) and `/search/docs/fundamentals/ai-optimization-guide` (**Last updated 2026-07-10**):

- "robots.txt directives for Googlebot is the control for site owners to manage access."
- "To be eligible to be shown as a supporting link in AI Overviews or AI Mode, a page must be indexed and eligible to be shown in Google Search with a snippet, fulfilling the Search technical requirements. **There are no additional technical requirements.**"
- "You don't need to create new machine readable files, AI text files, or markup to appear in these features… There's also no special schema.org structured data that you need to add."
- "Structured data isn't required for generative AI search."
- "There's no requirement to break your content into tiny pieces for AI to better understand it."
- On llms.txt (changelog **2026-06-15**): "these files aren't needed for Google Search (and won't negatively or positively impact your visibility or rankings)."
- `Google-Extended` "does not impact a site's inclusion in Google Search nor is it used as a ranking signal", and its scope list (Gemini training and grounding) **does not include AI Overviews or AI Mode** (google-common-crawlers, **2026-07-14**).
- Official material: "Top ways to ensure your content performs well in Google's AI experiences on Search", John Mueller, **May 21, 2025**; "A new resource for optimizing for generative AI", **May 15, 2026**; Search Generative AI performance reports, **June 3, 2026**, rolled out to all websites worldwide as of **August 31, 2026**; "spam policies apply to generative AI responses" changelog **May 15, 2026**.

## 1.9 Core Web Vitals and static performance facts

Nothing changed in the metric set. web.dev/articles/vitals lists three stable metrics, zero pending, zero experimental, and has not been edited since **2024-10-31**. CrUX release notes through August 2026 record no metric or threshold change.

| Metric | Good | Needs improvement | Poor | Source | Date | Class |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| LCP | <= 2.5 s | 2.5 to 4.0 s | > 4.0 s | https://web.dev/articles/lcp | 2025-09-04 | (a) |
| INP | <= 200 ms | > 200 to 500 ms | > 500 ms | https://web.dev/articles/inp | 2025-09-02 | (a) |
| CLS | <= 0.1 | > 0.1 to 0.25 | > 0.25 | https://web.dev/articles/cls | 2023-04-12 | (a) |

All at the **75th percentile**, segmented mobile and desktop (https://web.dev/articles/defining-core-web-vitals-thresholds, 2025-05-07). INP replaced FID: stable **2024-03-12**, FID support ended **2024-09-09**.

**Open Graph itself** (https://ogp.me/, no version and no date on the page, class (a)): four required properties, `og:title`, `og:type`, `og:image`, `og:url` ("The canonical URL of your object that will be used as its permanent ID in the graph"). `og:image:alt` is stated directly: "If the page specifies an og:image it should specify og:image:alt." Arrays repeat the tag and "The first tag (from top to bottom) is given preference during conflicts", with structured properties binding to the **most recently declared root tag**, so a parser that flattens `og:*` into a dict mis-reports multi-image pages. `og:locale` is `language_TERRITORY`, default `en_US`. Tags use `property=`, not `name=`. oEmbed discovery (https://oembed.com/) works through `<link rel="alternate" type="application/json+oembed">` **and** the HTTP `Link` header; `version` must be `1.0`.

**Binding constraint for one shared share image:** WhatsApp's 600 KB and <= 4:1, plus LinkedIn's 1200 x 627. A **1200 x 630 JPEG under 600 KB clears every documented requirement at once.** Use 600 KB as a warn threshold and 5 MB as a fail threshold. **No platform documents a title or description character limit**, so every "60 / 155 / 88 characters" rule is renderer folklore.

## 1.11 Security, DNS, mail and exposed files

| Fact | Auditor use | Source | Date | Class |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| HSTS grammar: `max-age` REQUIRED, `includeSubDomains` optional and valueless, each directive once, and a UA MUST ignore the **entire** header if any part violates the grammar | Parse strictly | RFC 6797 §6.1 | 2012-11 | (a) |
| A UA **MUST ignore** an HSTS header received over insecure transport, so reading HSTS off an `http://` response is a false pass. With more than one HSTS header, **only the first is processed** (the opposite of CSP, where all headers apply and intersect). HSTS is never noted for an IP-literal host | n/a | RFC 6797 §8.1 | 2012-11 | (a) |
| **`preload` is not in RFC 6797** (`grep -c -i preload` returns 0). It is defined only by hstspreload.org and Chromium's static list. hstspreload.org now argues against it: "While HSTS is recommended, HSTS *preloading* is not recommended," and tells tool authors "do not include the `preload` directive by default", while MDN's TLS guide still says to set it | Missing `preload` is **info**, never a finding | hstspreload.org ; MDN TLS guide | backing file committed 2025-01-23 ; 2026-08-15 | (a), sources conflict |
| hstspreload requirements: valid certificate; HTTP to HTTPS redirect on the same host; all subdomains over HTTPS; `max-age` at least `31536000` plus `includeSubDomains` plus `preload` | n/a | hstspreload.org | 2025-01-23 | (a) |
| `GET https://hstspreload.org/api/v2/status?domain=<d>` returns JSON with status in {unknown, pending, preloaded, rejected (deprecated), removed, pending-removal, pending-automated-removal}. **`google.com` returns `"unknown"` and that is correct**: the Chromium static list carries `accounts.google.com` and `mail.google.com` but no apex entry. `status: "unknown"` means "not in this submission database", not "not protected" | Never equate the two | verified live; Chromium `transport_security_state_static.json` (10.5 MB, 94,778 name occurrences) | 2026-09-21 | (a)/(b) |
| CSP: **multiple headers of either kind all apply and intersect.** `Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only` is not supported in `<meta>` at all, and `report-uri`, `frame-ancestors` and `sandbox` are stripped from a meta-delivered policy. A meta CSP that is not a child of `<head>` does nothing | **A site whose only clickjacking defence is `frame-ancestors` in a meta tag is unprotected.** High, silent, common | CSP3 WD §3.3, §6.3.2, §6.4.2; HTML Living Standard pragma | 2026-09-16 | (a) |
| `'strict-dynamic'` makes host-source and scheme-source expressions plus `'unsafe-inline'` and `'self'` **ignored** for script. Conversely, `'strict-dynamic'` with no nonce and no hash blocks all script | CSP3 §8.2, §6.7.3.2 | 2026-09-16 | (a) |

| Referrer-Policy browser default is `strict-origin-when-cross-origin`, so a **missing** header is at most info; `unsafe-url` is a real finding | n/a | MDN Referrer-Policy | 2026-09-04 | (a) |

Upgradable (auto-upgraded): `<img src>`, CSS image properties, `<audio src>`, `<video src>`, `<source>` for audio/video, **except when the host is an IP literal**, which is blocked. Blockable: `<script src>`, stylesheet `<link>`, `<iframe src>`, `fetch()`, XHR, CSS `url()` including `@font-face` and `cursor`, `<object>`, `sendBeacon()`, **`<img srcset>` and `<picture>`**, web fonts | `srcset` and `<picture>` behave differently from plain `img src` | MDN Mixed content | 2026-08-15 | (a) |

Void lookups (NOERROR-with-zero-answers or NXDOMAIN) **SHOULD** be limited to two. A DoH-based auditor can recurse and count this, which most auditors skip | The most valuable SPF check | RFC 7208 | 2014-04 | (a) |

Site reputation policy has an **EEA carve-out announced 2026-08-28, effective 2026-08-30** | Name the pattern, name the policy it resembles, state that intent is not determinable | https://developers.google.com/search/docs/essentials/spam-policies | 2026-08-28 | (a) |
| Link spam has the one crisp machine-checkable line: "It's not a violation of our policies to have such links as long as they are qualified with a `rel="nofollow"` or `rel="sponsored"` attribute value" | The only spam check with a clean rule | same | 2026-08-28 | (a) |
| Hidden text: explicit **non-violations** are accordions, tabs, sliders, tooltips, and "Text that's only accessible to screen readers" | Whitelist `.sr-only` and `.visually-hidden` or the check accuses well-built sites | same | 2026-08-28 | (a) |

# 2. Beliefs that are wrong or stale

Each of these makes an auditor confidently wrong. Encode them as negative rules.

## Stale facts to delete

1. **Googlebot fetches 2 MB, not 15 MB** (64 MB for PDF, applied to uncompressed data). 15 MB is only the default for crawlers that set no limit of their own.
2. **Favicon "must be a multiple of 48px" is stale.** Current rule: square, at least 8x8 px, recommend larger than 48x48. **SVG is not in the supported format list** (BMP, GIF, ICO, PNG, JPEG, PPM, TIFF), so "SVG favicons work in Google Search" is (c). The favicon must be crawlable by **Googlebot-Image** while the home page must be crawlable by **Googlebot**, two different tokens. One favicon per hostname.
3. **Google honors robots meta tags in the body**, not only in `<head>`. Never flag body placement.
4. **`Organization` and `Article` have no required properties.** `LocalBusiness` requires only `name` and `address`. `VideoObject` requires only `name`, `thumbnailUrl`, `uploadDate`.
5. **`priceRange` is not deprecated** on LocalBusiness. It is recommended, capped under 100 characters.
6. **`rel=next`/`rel=prev` are inert at Google**, so absence is never a finding. The real pagination bug is page 2+ canonicalizing to page 1.
7. **`rel=author` has been dead since 2014-08-28.** Mueller: "we're no longer processing this data -- it's not just a UI change."
8. **FAQ rich results ended 2026-05-07; HowTo ended 2023-09-13.** FAQPage and HowTo markup is inert, not erroneous. Report as dead weight, never as a defect.
9. **DMARC `pct` is historic** as of RFC 9989 (May 2026, obsoletes RFC 7489 and 9091). `np`, `psd` and `t` are the live additions. Flag `pct`'s presence, not a low value.
10. **WCAG 4.1.1 Parsing is obsolete and removed in WCAG 2.2.** Duplicate `id` is an HTML defect, never a 4.1.1 failure. **"Exactly one h1" is not a WCAG requirement** either.
11. **WCAG relative luminance uses 0.04045**, not the pre-May-2021 0.03928.
12. **X-Frame-Options is not deprecated.** The genuinely dead headers are `X-XSS-Protection: 1; mode=block` (MDN warns it creates vulnerabilities; only `0` is defensible), `Expect-CT`, `Feature-Policy`, `Public-Key-Pins`, and CSP `block-all-mixed-content`.
13. **`crawl-delay` is unsupported by Google but supported by Bing and Anthropic**, and explicitly unsupported by Amazon. It is not universally inert.
14. **`noarchive` and `nocache` are dead at Google but live and AI-meaningful at Bing.** Bing maps `noindex` to "no AI training", `noarchive` to "do not link in Chat and Copilot", `nocache` to "URL/snippet/title only", and `nocache` wins when both are present.
15. **Repoint Google crawling doc URLs** from `/search/docs/crawling-indexing/…` to `/crawling/docs/…` (moved November to December 2025).

## Parsing and protocol traps

16. **`hstspreload.org` `status: "unknown"` does not mean unprotected.** `google.com` returns `unknown` and is genuinely absent from the Chromium static list, which carries subdomains instead.
17. **RDAP status is `"client transfer prohibited"`**, space-separated lowercase, never EPP camelCase.
18. **Cloudflare DoH returns HTTP 400 without `Accept: application/dns-json`.**
19. **Long TXT records arrive as multiple quoted chunks in one `data` string. Join with NO separator.** Joining with a space corrupts SPF.
20. **"No MX" does not mean undeliverable** (RFC 5321 §5.1 implicit MX fallback to A/AAAA). Null MX (RFC 7505, preference 0, target `.`) does.
21. **DKIM selectors cannot be enumerated.** Report "unknown", never "missing".
22. **HSTS: only the first header counts, and it must be read over HTTPS.** CSP is the opposite, where all headers apply and intersect.
23. **`frame-ancestors`, `report-uri` and `sandbox` are stripped from a meta-delivered CSP**, and a meta CSP outside `<head>` is ignored entirely. A site whose only clickjacking defence is `frame-ancestors` in a meta tag is unprotected.
24. **Do not flag `https:` or `'unsafe-inline'` alongside `'strict-dynamic'`.** CSP3 §8.2 recommends them as fallback ballast, and `strict-dynamic` makes host-allowlist analysis meaningless.
25. **Do not use HEAD for byte-level facts.** RFC 9110 §9.3.2 permits omitting `Content-Length` and `Vary`; `www.google.com` omits `Content-Encoding` on HEAD, which reads as "uncompressed".
26. **`http.client` skips only status 100, so a `103` becomes the returned response** and desyncs the connection. Use a raw socket and count header sections.
27. **`http.client` pins `http/1.1` via ALPN in its own source**, so h2 support must be probed on a separate throwaway TLS connection with `set_alpn_protocols`.
28. **Probe robots.txt content type.** A `text/html` robots.txt is the most common real-world robots.txt bug, and it comes from a catch-all route.
29. **Always fetch a random-path control first** and compare hashes before reporting any exposed file. SPA and Worker catch-alls return identical bodies for every miss.
30. **`Content-Length` is usually absent on HTML** (chunked transfer). Count the bytes you read.
31. **Set a real User-Agent.** `Python-urllib/3.14` is 403'd by Cloudflare.
32. **`validator.schema.org/validate` responses are prefixed with the XSSI guard `)]}'`.** Strip it before `json.loads`.

## Interpretation traps

33. **`Google-Extended` does not control AI Overviews or AI Mode.** Googlebot access plus `nosnippet`, `max-snippet`, `data-nosnippet` and `noindex` do. But Grossman et al. measured that sites blocking Google-Extended got **zero** Gemini citations, so blocking it still has a real cost. Both halves of that sentence have to survive into the report.
34. **Cloudflare's managed robots.txt means the file you fetched is not the origin's.** Grep for `BEGIN Cloudflare Managed`.
35. **On a Cloudflare zone, bot blocking can vary page by page**, because "block only on pages that display ads" parses each page's HTML for ad units. A single-URL probe does not generalize.
36. **A UA-differential 403 is not proof a bot is blocked.** You are not on the bot's verified IP range. Report "differential response by User-Agent observed".
37. **Do not report "no CrUX data" as a performance finding on a noindexed site.** CrUX eligibility requires public discoverability, so a `noindex` page returns 404 by design.
38. **"AI Overview output analysis" is not "cited page analysis."** Surfer's "61% of AIOs contain a list" describes Google's generated answer, not the pages it cited.
39. **Never score "has schema" as AI visibility.** The only matched-control study found AI Overviews at -4.6% and nulls elsewhere, and Google documents no effect.
40. **Never flag a missing `/llms.txt`.** 97% of existing ones got zero requests in May 2026, and no AI bot probes for a nonexistent one.
41. **IndexNow setup is not externally verifiable.** The key filename is the secret, there is no `.well-known` path, and blind endpoint probes return 429 regardless of the target. Require owner attestation.
42. **Do not recommend pinging Bing after a sitemap update.** `bing.com/ping?sitemap=` returns 410.
43. **Microsoft documents no Copilot crawler token.** Copilot rides bingbot.
44. **Absence of `msvalidate.01` does not mean the site is unverified.** Three of Bing's four verification methods leave no HTML trace.
45. **X publishes no Cards documentation in 2026.** Its numbers survive only in dated Wayback snapshots. Emit the tags, grade them low, and say the behaviour is untestable without posting.
46. **Only Slack, Meta and WhatsApp document their fetch mechanics.** No platform documents issuing a HEAD request. "Unfurlers use HEAD" is folklore.
47. **Slack ignores robots.txt entirely** ("We do not currently honor `robots.txt` files"), and `facebookexternalhit` and `meta-externalfetcher` may bypass it.
48. **Facebook accepts only gzip and deflate.** A Brotli-only origin breaks Facebook unfurling.
49. **The binding og:image constraints are WhatsApp's 600 KB and 4:1 or less, plus LinkedIn's 1200x627.** A 1200x630 JPEG under 600 KB clears every documented requirement at once.
50. **A numeric spam score built from HTML features is fabrication.** Every Google spam policy except the `rel` rule on paid links turns on intent, and the permitted `.sr-only` idiom is byte-identical to the banned off-screen-text pattern.
51. **If the auditor scrapes SERPs, the auditor is the spam-policy violator**, not the site. Google's machine-generated-traffic policy names "scraping results for rank-checking purposes".
52. **Severity calibration.** AI referral traffic is about 1% of site traffic (Conductor 2026-07-06, 1,215 enterprise domains; Ahrefs 0.25% across 81,947 sites). AI-search findings should not outrank crawlability or Core Web Vitals in the severity ordering.

## A note on the `&num=100` story

The removal of Google's results-per-page parameter around **September 10 to 12, 2025** is class **(b)**: well corroborated by trade press and tool vendors, never confirmed by Google. There is no Search Central blog post, zero occurrences of "num=100" in the full changelog, nothing in the Search Status Dashboard between the August 2025 spam update (26 Aug 2025) and a serving issue (3 Oct 2025), and no Search Console data anomaly. The only official utterance is a spokesperson quote relayed by Search Engine Land (Barry Schwartz, **September 18, 2025**): "The use of this URL parameter is not something that we formally support." Causal explanations are (c); the circulating impression-drop percentages (87.7% / 77.6%) are (b) at best from a single unfetched analysis. **Auditor implication: none directly.** It only makes Search Console impression baselines discontinuous around 2025-09-10.

# 3. What the evidence says about GEO and AEO content tactics

The literature has a load-bearing structural flaw. Nearly every positive result measures what happens to a document **already placed in the model's context**, then gets reported as if it were a result about getting retrieved in the first place. When researchers built end-to-end pipelines including retrieval and reranking, the same tactics turned **negative**. The best-controlled industry study on the most popular tactic (schema markup) found **no effect**. Google's own current documentation is explicitly deflationary.

## 3.1 The academic core

|---|---|---|---|---|

The abstract's "up to 40%" is Quotation Addition's PAWC figure | **(b), context-only.** No result speaks to retrieval |

## 3.2 Schema markup and AI citation: the matched-control result

**Ahrefs, "We Tracked 1,885 Pages Adding Schema"** (`ahrefs.com/blog/schema-ai-citations/`, Linehan with Guan, reviewed by Ryan Law, JSON-LD `datePublished` **2026-05-11**). From about 6M URLs cited in AI Overviews, crawler HTML history was labelled for `<script type="application/ld+json">` and the False-to-True transition dated. **1,885 treated pages** against **4,000 matched controls** (3 per treated page, different domains, similar pre-period citation levels), 30 days pre and post, **matched difference-in-differences**:

| Platform | Effect | Significance |
|---|---|---|
| Google AI Overviews | **-4.6%** | significant, "about 1 in 2,500" by chance |
| Google AI Mode | +2.4% | indistinguishable from zero |
| ChatGPT | +2.2% | indistinguishable from zero |

Conclusion verbatim: "For pages already getting cited by AI, adding JSON-LD schema didn't boost citations on Google AI Mode or ChatGPT, and showed only a small decline in AI Overviews that we can't clearly attribute to schema." Stated limitations: all pages already had 100+ AIO citations, schema types were pooled, 30-day window, HTML-embedded JSON-LD only, Perplexity not measured. The same article reports the correlational version people quote out of context (AI-cited pages were about 3x more likely to have JSON-LD, 53% of cited pages have schema) and calls it confounded: "Schema markup tends to live on better-maintained, more technically sophisticated sites." **The conflict of interest runs the wrong way: Ahrefs sells AI-visibility tooling and published a null, which raises its credibility.** Strength: **(b), the best-controlled study in the field.**

Mechanism tests pointing the same way. **searchVIU** ("Schema markup and AI in 2025", published 2025-12-02, tested 2025-10-30): one synthetic page, prices in 8 conditions, each system queried 5 times. Gemini found 4/8 and was the **only system that executed JavaScript**; ChatGPT 3/8 (visible HTML plus visible Microdata and RDFa, no JS, **ignored all hidden schema**); Google AI Mode 2/8; Perplexity 1/8; Claude 0/8. **The JSON-LD-only price was found by none of the five.** n=1 page, and the authors correctly note schema "could very well be used in earlier phases". **Mark Williams-Cook** (2026-05-28) built a page whose address existed only inside JSON-LD with a non-resolving `@context`, an invented `@type` and zero real schema.org properties; ChatGPT and Perplexity both returned it, and Perplexity volunteered that it found it in the structured data. His own limit: "A system that consulted schema and fell back to text extraction would produce the same answer here." The tokenization argument (that pre-training pipelines strip `<script>`) is reasoning, not measurement, so **(c)** for the mechanism and **(b)** at small n for the result.

**The pro-schema literature does not hold up.** OtterlyAI (2026-03-23) tested **three pages on Otterly's own site**, 319 prompts, 7 platforms, **no control group**, and reported ChatGPT -71%, AIO +611%, AI Mode +42%, Gemini -35%, Perplexity 0%, Copilot -64%. That spread is a noise distribution, and Otterly sells AI-visibility tracking. Catalogued second-hand via Daniel Cheung's review (the underlying studies were not opened, so all of it is second-hand): AirOps x Indig, 16,851 queries, a 6.5-point gap with no retrieval-rank control; GEO-16's "+39% structured data lift" on a corpus of already-cited pages with no uncited comparison group; Digital Applied (April 2026, 5,000 sites, r=0.34, no controls, and incidentally **49% of schema fails validation**); SearchAtlas (2025-12-14, buckets indistinguishable); Fischman 2026 (730 AI citations, **null after rank correction**, 61.7% with rich schema vs 59.8% with none); Schema App and Evertune positive claims with no disclosed methodology. **The widely circulated BrightEdge "44%" schema figure does not exist**; the real BrightEdge 44% concerned AI Overviews criticising brands. The "Microsoft confirmed schema helps its LLMs" claim is **(c)**, built on trade-press coverage of an SMX Munich remark by Fabrice Canel in March 2025, not a Bing document.

Google's own position, from the ai-features doc (2025-12-10) and the ai-optimization-guide (2026-07-10): "There's also no special schema.org structured data that you need to add", and "overfocusing on structured data" is listed as unnecessary. The only structured-data instruction on either page is "Making sure your structured data matches the visible text on the page."

## 3.3 Off-page dominance, measured

| Study | Date | Sample | Result | Strength |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **SE Ranking AI Mode citation drivers** (Yulia Deda) | 2025-12-15 | **2,328,533 pages / 295,485 domains / 20 niches / 500,000+ prompts, XGBoost with SHAP attribution** | Median citations by bucket: **domain traffic 2.4 to 6.4**, **referring domains 2.5 to 6.8**, homepage traffic 3.6 to 6.5, content length 4.1 to 5.1, freshness 3.9 to 5.0, FAQ block 4.4 to 4.9, section length best at 100 to 150 words (4.7), readability 4.0 (FK grade 11+) to 4.6 (grade 6 to 8), **LCP 4.4 (>2.65 s) to 4.9 (0.2 to 1.02 s)**. **FAQ schema markup had "three times weaker" effect than the actual FAQ content** | **(b), the only real multivariate attribution.** SHAP attributes variance in a fitted model, not causation, and the study does not account for query fan-out |
| SE Ranking companion, ChatGPT | 2025-11-24 | 129,000 domains / 216,524 pages / 100,000 prompts | "Pages with an average section length of 120 to 180 words perform best, with 4.6 citations", and "70% more ChatGPT citations than pages with sections under 50 words". **The baseline is sub-50-word fragments and every downstream post drops it.** Also: **including llms.txt as a feature reduced model accuracy** | (b) |
| Ahrefs branded-mentions correlation (Linehan with Guan) | 2025-05-26 | 75,000 brands, Spearman | **Branded web mentions rho 0.664**, branded anchors 0.527, branded search volume 0.392, DR 0.326, referring domains 0.295, branded traffic 0.274, **backlinks 0.218**. Follow-up 2025-12-12 puts **YouTube mentions above web mentions**: 0.737 ChatGPT, 0.740 AI Mode, 0.712 AIO | **(b) weak.** Filtered to DR>40 and a keyword at 800+ searches, so it studies already-large brands; about 26% with zero AIO mentions were **dropped**, truncating the variance that would test the hypothesis; both variables proxy brand size. **"Brand mentions beat backlinks 3-to-1" is (c): dividing two Spearman coefficients is not a valid operation** |
| Profound | 2026-07-30 | **11.84 billion citations**, 2026-04-16 to 2026-07-16, eight models | **About 57% of citations are brand-owned sites.** ChatGPT lowest at 47%, **Gemini highest at 69%**. Cybersecurity 74%, government and nonprofit 15.9% | **(b) with a serious unstated bias:** the prompt population is Profound's customer configuration set, a convenience sample skewed toward brands that bought AEO monitoring. Still the strongest justification for a page-side audit existing at all |
| The "Reddit, Wikipedia and YouTube dominate" story | n/a | n/a | **Pew (independent, non-vendor), 2025-07-22, 68,879 searches, 900 US adults: all three combined are 15% of AIO sources** (vs 17% of standard results). SE Ranking 2024-07-11: Reddit and Quora **0 links each**. Semrush 2025-11-10 (230K prompts): Reddit went from about 60% of ChatGPT responses to about 10% **in six weeks**. Ahrefs 2026-09-02 (3M+ queries): YouTube 22.9%, Reddit 18.5%, Wikipedia 4.0%, but that is **share among the top 50 sources**, a different denominator. Ahrefs 2026-04-15 (1.4M prompts): Reddit is retrieved constantly but **cited 1.93%** | **The domination story is an artefact of top-50 share metrics plus one mid-2025 window that ended abruptly. No audit should hard-code "get on Reddit"** |
| Seer review-profile study (Nick Haigler) | 2026-05-14 | 804,491 AI responses, 1,926 brands | Median citation rate 1% (no Trustpilot profile) to 53.5% (1 to 13 reviews). **Commissioned by Trustpilot.** A 1% to 53.5% jump from as few as one review is not a plausible causal effect of the review; it proxies "this brand exists commercially at scale" | **downgrade toward (c)** |

## 3.4 Top-10 overlap: there is no single answer, and the spread is definitional

| Source | Date | Sample | Engine | Denominator | Result |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| SE Ranking | 2024-06-03 | 100,013 kw | AIO | AIOs with at least one top-10 domain | 84.72% |
| SE Ranking | 2024-07-11 | 100,013 kw | AIO | same, Labs disabled | 93.67% |
| SE Ranking | 2024-07-11 | 100,013 kw | AIO | **all links** in top 1 to 100 | 56.50% (about 41% from the top 10) |
| Ahrefs | 2025-07-21 | 1.9M citations / 1M AIOs | AIO | **top-3 most visible citations only** | **76.10%** |
| Ahrefs | 2025-08-11 | 15,000 long-tail | ChatGPT | all citations vs Google top 10 | **8.0%** |
| Ahrefs | 2025-08-11 | 15,000 long-tail | Perplexity / Gemini / Copilot | same | 28.6% / 8.6% / 8.2% |
| BrightEdge | 2025-09-18 | **n not stated** | AIO | all citations, top 10 | 16.7% |
| **Ahrefs** | **2026-03-02** | **863K SERPs / 4M AIO URLs** | AIO | **all citations** | **top 10 37.9%, 11 to 100 31.2%, beyond 100 31.0%** |
| Surfer | updated 2026-09-17 | 405,576 AIOs | AIO | cited sources in top 10 | 52% |
| Xu et al. (academic) | 2026-05 | 55,393 queries | AIO | AIO reference domains | **41.4% top 10, 70.2% full page 1** |

**The 76% to 38% "collapse" is largely an artefact.** The 2025 study analysed the top 3 most visible citations; the 2026 study analysed all 4M. Ahrefs attributes the change to query fan-out and Gemini
3. Anyone selling this as "AI decoupled from rankings in eight months" is over-reading a denominator change. **Best defensible statement:** for AI Overviews, roughly a third to 40% of citations come from the classic top 10, roughly a third from 11 to 100, and roughly a third from nowhere in the top
100. For standalone ChatGPT, overlap with Google's top 10 for the typed query is under 10%, but fan-out means the typed query is the wrong baseline and nobody has measured against the expanded set. **Ranking top 10 is neither necessary nor sufficient for citation**, so an AI-search audit section must not be a repackaged rank-readiness checklist.

## 3.5 JavaScript rendering: the Vercel claim and how it is misquoted

**Source:** "The rise of the AI crawler", `vercel.com/blog/the-rise-of-the-ai-crawler`, Giacomo Zecchini, Alice Alexandra Moore, Malte Ubl, Ryan Siddle, **published 2024-12-17**, on Vercel's blog only.

**The real methodology statement:** "Our primary data comes from monitoring nextjs.org and the Vercel network for the past few months," validated on Resume Library and CV Library. **There is no stated N for the rendering test, no stated date range, and no description of how JS execution was detected in logs.** The widely repeated "they analysed 500 million GPTBot fetches and found zero JS execution" is a **secondary-source fabrication** that retrofits the 569M monthly volume figure onto the rendering claim. Copilot was excluded for lacking a unique UA, and **bingbot is not mentioned anywhere in the article.**

**Verdict, verbatim:** "none of the major AI crawlers currently render JavaScript. This includes: OpenAI (OAI-SearchBot, ChatGPT-User, GPTBot); Anthropic (ClaudeBot); Meta (Meta-ExternalAgent); ByteDance (Bytespider); Perplexity (PerplexityBot)," plus CCBot. Exceptions: "Google's Gemini leverages Googlebot's infrastructure, enabling full JavaScript rendering" and AppleBot "renders JavaScript through a browser-based crawler." Fetch but do not execute: ChatGPT 11.50% and Claude 23.84% of requests are JavaScript files. **The caveat the industry drops:** "content included in the initial HTML response, like JSON data or delayed React Server Components, may still be indexed since AI models can process non-rendered content." Also reported: **ChatGPT wastes 34.82% of its fetches on 404s.**

**Strength: (b), and date-stamped December 2024.** It was never re-run by its authors and is restated everywhere as current fact. The only independent corroboration is searchVIU's n=1 test from October 2025, which agrees. Neither is a replication at scale. **Platform documentation is silent:** OpenAI's bots doc, Anthropic's support article and Perplexity's crawler doc contain zero mentions of JavaScript. Bing's only rendering statement is from **2018** (Canel and Dubut, 2018-10-31: "bingbot is generally able to render JavaScript" but "it is difficult for bingbot to process JavaScript at scale on every page of every website"), eight years old and never superseded. **`Google-Extended` is a robots.txt token with no HTTP user agent, so it fetches nothing, and every "Google-Extended renders JavaScript" sentence is a category error.**

**Brave, which is what Claude actually searches.** MERJ, "How Brave Search discovers new pages", Ryan Siddle with Josh Blyskal (Profound), **2026-07-09**: "When Claude searches the web, Brave Search does the searching, according to Google Cloud's documentation for Anthropic's models. Across roughly 35,000 Claude citations analysed by Profound, 79.2% of Claude's cited URLs appear in Brave's top 10 for the matching query, compared with 34% for Google's top 10." Brave's verification fetch, traced to source at commit `f25eb3d`: **never executes JavaScript, honours `noindex` and canonical only in the HTML (never HTTP headers), rejects any redirect, gives up beyond 10 seconds or 2 MB.** Discovery requires about 20 distinct opted-in users on different networks, or one user viewing a Google, Bing, Yahoo or DuckDuckGo results page where you already rank. **No sitemap submission, no IndexNow.** Conflict: the citation dataset is Profound's, MERJ advertises a Profound partnership, and it is not independently auditable. The code tracing is **(b)** and verifiable. **This is the only documented AI-fetcher timeout and size limit anywhere.**

**Crawl volume, for context.** Cloudflare fixed-cohort, "From Googlebot to GPTBot", **2025-07-01**, May 2024 vs May 2025: Googlebot 30% to 50% share (+96% raw), Bingbot 10% to 8.7% (+2%), GPTBot 2.2% to 7.7% (**+305%**), ClaudeBot 11.7% to 5.4% (**-46%**), Bytespider 22.8% to 2.9% (**-85%**), ChatGPT-User 0.1% to 1.3%, PerplexityBot under 0.01% to 0.2%. **Botify / Nectiv** (Chris Long, **about 7 billion OpenAI bot log events** isolated from a 250-billion-event corpus, **Nov 2024 to Mar 2026**): OpenAI crawl roughly tripled after GPT-5 (OAI-SearchBot about 3.5x, GPTBot about 2.9x), and **OAI-SearchBot now out-logs GPTBot**. **Retrieval-at-answer-time now exceeds training crawl, so blocking OAI-SearchBot removes you from live answers and is a more immediate harm than blocking GPTBot.** Weaknesses: Botify enterprise clients only, crawl volume is not citation volume, and no statement on reverse-DNS verification of spoofable UAs. Cloudflare robots.txt adoption data (2025-06-06): of the top 10,000 domains, robots.txt found on 3,816, and **546 (about 14%)** carried AI-bot-specific directives, with **GPTBot both the most disallowed (312 domains) and the most explicitly allowed (61)**.

**Documented robots.txt non-compliance.** Cloudflare, 2025-08-04: brand-new unindexed domains with full-deny robots.txt plus WAF rules blocking PerplexityBot and Perplexity-User still returned page-specific content to Perplexity; an undeclared crawler presenting a generic Chrome/124 macOS UA was observed at **3 to 6M daily requests**, rotating IPs outside the published range and rotating ASNs. Cloudflare de-listed Perplexity as a verified bot; the same test on OpenAI led OpenAI to stop. **Caveats: Cloudflare sells the blocking product, the detection method is not externally reproducible, and Perplexity disputed the characterisation.** An HTML auditor cannot test any of this, so do not encode it.

## 3.6 llms.txt: the log evidence

**The spec** (https://llmstxt.org/, Jeremy Howard, published 2024-09-03, modified 2026-08-10) requires an H1 with the site name as "the only required section", then optionally a blockquote summary, markdown detail sections, H2-delimited file lists of `[name](url)` items, and an `## Optional` section for links an agent can skip. It also proposes `.md` URL twins discovered via `<link rel="alternate" type="text/markdown">`. **`llms-full.txt` is a community convention, not part of the spec as fetched.**

**The measurement that ends the argument. Ahrefs, Louise Linehan, 2026-06-15: 137,210 domains, server-log data, May 2026.** 28% adoption, stated as an upper bound because "Ahrefs customers skew more technical and SEO-aware than the web at large". **97% of those files received zero traffic in May 2026.** Of the 3% with any requests, 96% were bots and only 19.5% of fetches came from named AI tools. The decisive line: **"Zero requests came from AI bots for llms.txt files that don't exist. They never go looking."** A crawler that used llms.txt would probe for it and generate 404s. There are none. Strength **(b), strong design for a negative.**

Corroborating: Originality.ai tracked 3M+ websites June 2025 to May 2026 and saw llms.txt instances grow 4,088 to 36,120 (8.8x), while **SEO audit tools were 21.7% of requests to those files** and AI retrieval bots 1.1% (reported at ppc.land, **2026-07-02**, secondary reporting of two vendor studies). SE Ranking found that including llms.txt as a model feature **reduced accuracy**. Mueller, Reddit, **2025-04-17**: "AFAIK none of the AI services have said they're using LLMs.TXT (and you can tell when you look at your server logs that they don't even check for it)… To me, it's comparable to the keywords meta tag." Mueller on Bluesky via SER **2026-01-20**, asked whether Google's own `ai.google.dev/api/llms.txt` is an endorsement: **"to be direct, no."**

**Publishing an llms.txt is not consuming one.** OpenAI, Anthropic and Google all publish llms.txt on their developer-docs sites because their docs platforms generate them automatically. **None of them documents their crawlers reading other sites' llms.txt.** This is the single most abused fact in GEO marketing.

**One real consumer exists, and it is a linter.** Lighthouse 13.3 (released **2026-05-07**, Chrome 150+) added an **Agentic Browsing** category with an audit checking for an llms.txt and whether it is missing an H1, too short, or has no links. The category is scored as a **pass-ratio, not a 0 to 100 weighted score** (https://developer.chrome.com/docs/lighthouse/agentic-browsing/scoring, page shows 2026-05-05). Other audits cover WebMCP tool registration, agent-centric accessibility and CLS. Exact audit ids are unverified.

**Other agent-discovery surfaces, for completeness.** Only `security.txt` (RFC 9116) and `robots.txt` (RFC 9309) are actual standards; say so rather than implying parity. A2A agent cards moved from `/.well-known/agent.json` (v0.2.x) to `/.well-known/agent-card.json` (v0.3.0+), a genuine migration, class (a). MCP server discovery is **not standardized**: three competing proposals (SEP-1649, SEP-2127, SEP-1960) plus an individual IETF draft, unsettled by the 2026-07-28 spec release candidate. WebMCP (`navigator.modelContext`) is a **W3C Community Group** draft report (2026-02-10, updated 2026-04-23), **not on the Standards Track**. `agents.json` is one vendor at v0.1.0. NLWeb exists with thin adoption. Agentic Commerce Protocol (OpenAI and Stripe) is real but **feed-based, with nothing in a merchant's HTML to check**. `ai.txt` has multiple incompatible proposals, no standards-body adoption and no confirmed crawler enforcement, class (c). TDMRep (`/.well-known/tdmrep.json`) is a W3C Community Group **Final Report 2024-05-10, explicitly "not a W3C Standard nor on the W3C Standards Track"**, but has legal weight in the EU under Art. 4 of the DSM Directive; measured adoption is **28 of 7,282 observed hosts (0.38%)** in a frozen 10,667-host sample, September 2026.

## 3.7 Freshness, structure and speed

**Freshness has the strongest documented basis of any content check.** Google's byline-dates doc (`/appearance/publication-dates`, **2025-12-10**): "Google doesn't depend on a single date factor"; "Add a user-visible date to the page and feature it prominently"; "specify the `datePublished` and/or `dateModified` fields"; **"Make your dates and times consistent. Ensure that the date (and optional time and timezone) match between the equivalent user-visible and structured values"**; "Don't specify future dates"; "Minimize the presence of other dates on the page." The anti-faking language is in creating-helpful-content (2025-12-10): "Are you changing the date of pages to make them seem fresh when the content has not substantially changed?"

Measured: **Ahrefs, 2025-07-28, 16.975 million cited URLs** across ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, Copilot and AIO vs organic SERPs. AI-cited content averaged **1,064 days** old vs organic **1,432 days**, a 25.7% gap; ChatGPT's citations were **458 days newer**; **and the finding nobody quotes, Google AI Overviews cited content 16 days *older* than organic.** The average cited page is still 2.9 years old. Weakness: age derives from dates the pages declare, so the sample is restricted to date-exposing pages and inherits any date inflation, with no topic control. Seer (2025-06-25, 5,000+ URLs) found 65% / 79% / 89% / 94% of hits within 1 / 2 / 3 / 5 years but **provides no base rate**, without which the figure means little. Strength **(b)**.

**Structure evidence is thin and contradictory.** Growth Memo (Kevin Indig, 2026-03-23) reports 44.2% of LLM citations from the first 30% of text, 31.1% middle, 24.7% final third, but **the primary is paywalled and unverified**, its two secondary sample descriptions conflict ("1.2 million AI answers and 18,012 verified citations" vs "3 million ChatGPT responses and 30 million citations, isolating 18,012"), and **uniform distribution would put 30% in the first 30%, so 44.2% is a 1.47x over-representation** while the bottom 30% still earns a quarter of citations. A claimed "41% vs 29% citation rate for question-form headlines" has no locatable primary. Claims of "2.8x more likely" and "68.7% of ChatGPT-cited pages followed sequential heading structure from 12,000+ URLs", attributed to an AirOps page, were checked: **those numbers are not on that page at all. The attribution was fabricated somewhere in the chain.** The closest real evidence is **GEO16** (arXiv:2509.10762, Kumar and Palkhouski, 2025-09-13): 70 product-intent prompts, 1,702 citations, 1,100 URLs, English B2B SaaS, logistic models with domain-clustered standard errors, finding metadata and freshness, semantic HTML and structured data most associated with citation. Severe weaknesses: tiny prompt set, one vertical, observational, and the predictors are **banded composite pillar scores**, so headings cannot be isolated. Against it, the best-sampled feature analysis found **Q&A format at -5.74%**.

**On tables and lists there is nothing.** Surfer's 405,576 AI Overviews (page updated 2026-09-17) finding 61% unordered lists, 12% ordered, 6% both, 21% none, plus 157-word average AIOs with 5 sources, **measures the format of Google's generated answer, not the format of the pages it cited.** Semrush's 200,000-keyword AIO study made the same error and analysed no source-page HTML. Claims like "tables boost citations 28 to 40%", "a table is cited 34% more often than prose", "tables achieve an 81% extraction rate vs 23% for paragraphs" are all **(c)**. **No verifiable study compared the presence of `<table>` or `<ul>` in cited versus non-cited pages.**

**Length contradicts itself.** SE Ranking says 120 to 180-word sections perform best against a sub-50-word baseline. **Ahrefs** (Despina Gavoyannis, 2025-12-03, 560,346 AIOs to 1,677,876 cited URLs to 174,048 pages with boilerplate-stripped word counts) found the average cited page at **1,282 words**, **53.4% under 1,000 words**, and **Spearman between word count and citation position of 0.04, "essentially zero"**, concluding "content length alone won't get you cited". Academic chunking work undercuts the premise entirely: arXiv:2505.21700 finds 64 to 128 tokens optimal for concise factual answers and 512 to 1024 for broader context, **varying by embedding model**, and arXiv:2504.19754 finds neither late chunking nor contextual retrieval uniformly beats fixed-size. **Optimal chunk size is a property of the retriever inside the platform.** Google: "There's no requirement to break your content into tiny pieces."

**Google cannot be opted into featured snippets.** Verbatim, answering how to mark up a page to be a featured snippet: **"You can't. Google systems determine whether a page would make a good featured snippet."** Only opt-out exists. Passage ranking (announced 2020-10-15, projected to improve 7% of queries, live 2021-02-10) already finds the buried passage for you, which reduces rather than increases the need to restructure.

**Speed and AI citation is folklore with one real mechanism inside it.** The only study, Dan Taylor (SALT.agency), Search Engine Land, January 2026, **cannot be opened (HTTP 403)**; secondary reports give 107,352 pages, **LCP r = -0.12 to -0.18**, CLS r = -0.05 to -0.09, with the author concluding vitals are a constraint rather than a growth lever. Even at face value r about -0.15 is fully consistent with confounding through ranking, and SE Ranking's multivariate model shows LCP moving citations 4.4 to 4.9 while domain traffic moves them 2.4 to 6.4. **No AI platform documents any performance threshold**: OpenAI's, Perplexity's and Anthropic's crawler docs contain no fetch timeout, no rate limit, no latency requirement and no caching policy, so every circulating number ("1 to 5 second timeouts", "TTFB under 2 seconds", "200 ms and crawlers reduce request rate") is **(c)**. The single documented timeout anywhere is Brave's 10 seconds and 2 MB. The HTTP 499 story (implicator.ai, "some sites see this error on 5% of ChatGPT crawler visits") has no logs, no site list, no sample size and no date range, so it is **(c)**, but the underlying mechanism is real and worth stating: **a 499 from an AI fetcher means the client hung up before the server finished, so the model got nothing. That is a binary retrieval failure, not a graded speed signal.**

## 3.8 Trust, authorship and entity signals

The Search Quality Rater Guidelines were verified by direct download: `https://guidelines.raterhub.com/searchqualityevaluatorguidelines.pdf`, HTTP 200, **8,969,290 bytes, 182 pages, titled "General Guidelines / September 11, 2025."** §0.1 verbatim: **"No single rating can directly impact how a particular webpage, website, or result appears in Google Search… Instead, ratings are used to measure how effectively search engines are working."** It is a rating rubric for contract evaluators. It does not describe a signal. §3.4: "Trust is the most important member of the E-E-A-T family." §2.5.3: "Contact information and customer service information are extremely important for websites that handle money." §4.5: "YMYL pages or websites that handle sensitive data with absolutely no information about the website or content creator should be rated Lowest." §4.5.1 is titled "Inadequate Information about the Website or Content Creator for the Purpose of the Page." It also flags conflict of interest: "'reviews' by the product manufacturer ('Our product is great!')… are not as trustworthy," which lines up exactly with the self-serving review rule.

Google states plainly that **E-E-A-T is not a ranking factor**: "While E-E-A-T itself isn't a specific ranking factor, using a mix of factors that can identify content with good E-E-A-T is useful," and "Rater data is not used directly in our ranking algorithms" (creating-helpful-content, 2025-12-10). Its actual author guidance is about **visible bylines, not markup**: "Do pages carry a byline, where one might be expected? Do bylines lead to further information about the author?" and "We strongly encourage adding accurate authorship information."

**No measured-effect literature exists** for Person schema, `sameAs`, `legalName`, contact or address markup, About pages or editorial-policy pages, on either AI citation or Google rankings. Nothing surfaced across roughly a dozen searches, which is "nothing surfaced", not proof of absence; the research session's search budget ran out before a final sweep. The one adjacent academic result, **AttriBench** (arXiv:2604.05224, 2026-04-06), evaluates 11 LLMs on quote attribution and finds large systematic disparities by race, gender and intersectional group plus a **suppression** failure mode where models omit attribution even with authorship information available. That is a fairness result about models, not a publisher-side lever.

**The defensible version:** a missing About page, missing contact information and missing bylines on a money-handling site are what Google's own published rater rubric treats as marks of an untrustworthy site, and they are cheap to fix. That is a reasoned recommendation grounded in a published rubric. It is **not** a measured ranking effect and must never be presented as one.

| Ahrefs | 2025-02-06 | 3,000 sites | AI = 0.12% of views, 0.17% of visitors; 63% of sites got at least one AI visit |
